rv.q: And I found this great American actor to be deeply affecting at the core of Cromer’s powerful production, his lean body and craggy features contorting into a complicated, scarred and fundamentally likable character who constantly has to motivate himself to draw another breath.
However, it also feels tonally bumpy by the end.

Still, when The Fear of 13 finally arrives at something close to Nick’s Rosebud revelation, we’re meant to connect the dots between past trauma and current predicament, and it is a tenuous connection at best, a possible cause for an effect we’ve been told repeatedly to distrust.
But he’s so enamored with that bravado, that of his character and his own, that he only glancingly finds a dimension beyond it.

While Mr. Brody has a lithe, lanky and compelling presence, he can bring only limited bursts of animation to a play that never gains much dramatic propulsion, a liability of its oppressive setting and the slow trudge of the narrative.
But at the James Earl Jones, which is four times the size, the distance makes those wrong notes echo.
It is polite theater that soothes rather than sears.
It’s just that “The Fear of 13,” as written, is a lifeless, stuffy and dutiful schlep through years of events, posing an insurmountable obstacle for any actor.
No, The Fear of 13 isn’t bad, and you can pay hundreds of dollars to see it onstage if you like.
But on stage, it’s an awkward mix, with a lot of monotonously earnest direct address and too few dramatized scenes to lend it vitality.
Affecting a slightly bent and not entirely confident gait, Brody—who bears no resemblance to the bald Yarris of the documentary—can’t be faulted in the least for his portrayal.
On stage, he’s a real theater animal and his performance is immeasurably enhanced by a face and body that rivet an audience’s attention for two straight hours.
He brings all this to bear in a performance that goes beyond the thrill of seeing a movie star’s first time on stage.
“The Fear of 13” works best as a showcase for its leading man and excellent featured actors.
Fortunately, Adrien Brody is so powerful as Nick Yarris and David Cromer’s direction is so tight, the play succeeds more than it should.

Strong performances by Adrien Brody and Tessa Thompson elevate this onstage look at the life of Nick Yarris, but that doesn’t free The Fear of 13 from its extended stretches of theatrical and emotional lockup.

That may be enough, but I would argue that this dramatic retelling would be better served if it were to provide more of the complexity of the case, or even some well-structured fictionalized embellishment.
But despite its good intentions and powerful true-life story, The Fear of 13 fails to galvanize.
The Fear of 13, which fails to explicate how Nick's false murder accusation boomerangs on him, leading to his conviction.

Adapting liberally from British filmmaker David Sington’s 2015 documentary of the same name, playwright Lindsey Ferrentino turns the true story of Nick Yarris–a Pennsylvania man who served an unjust 22-year death row sentence for rape and murder–into something that feels decidedly less true.

Much of this, as in Versailles, is due to the multiplicity of voices she admits into her storytelling; a keystone of documentaries’ allowance of real people to say their piece, but a tactic that typically muddles dramatic coherence.
But these key assets are far from enough to turn “The Fear of 13” into a 10.

I kept wondering if his irresistible charm was leading me to incredulously believe a story that seems too good to be true (a note at the top of the film assures us that everything has been independently verified).
Adrien Brody and Tessa Thompson making their Broadway debuts may be reason enough to go, even when Ferrentino's play asks you to wait for a payoff that arrives later than it should.
But this remains a very talky, exposition-heavy narrative that gets fuzzy whenever the spotlight shifts to somebody other than Nick.
Lindsey Ferrentino’s overpowering new work, based on the true story of a man named Nick Yarris, who served twenty-one years on death row for a murder he didn’t commit.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats

vr.q: He has these long, distinctive facial features that carry a childlike charisma just as easily as a devastating sorrow... he doesn't leave the stage for the entire two hours, carrying the show with a delicateness and commitment to the text that's undoubtedly very technical, but flows out of him like a song.
